content: 1. Regardless of whether you have received treatment or not, where would you prefer to receive your treatment? You may select up to three options: hospital, HIV clinic, drug user support center, community-based organization center, sexual and reproductive health clinics, general practitioner’s office, the same site as the testing location, no preference, or other (please specify). 2. What are the most important factors for you when considering locations for hepatitis C treatment? You may select up to three options: proximity to home or workplace, service hours, waiting time, direct costs (e.g., treatment and healthcare worker fees), indirect costs (e.g., loss of wages, transportation), confidence in personnel, presence of community or peer workers, presence of community-friendly medical personnel, a non-stigmatizing and non-judgmental approach, anonymity (a place where you can avoid being recognized by someone you know), no preference, none of the above, or other (please specify). 3. If your viral load is positive, indicating an active hepatitis C infection, when would you prefer to start treatment? Options include the same day, the next day, several days later, a few weeks later, or more than a few weeks later. Please provide comments. 4. Would you prefer to be tested and receive treatment at the same location? Options include yes, no, or I don’t know. Please provide comments. 5. If you answered yes to the previous question, what is the main reason for your preference? Options include a community-friendly site, convenience, avoiding additional administrative procedures, continued follow-up from testing to treatment, or other (please specify). Please provide comments. 6. If you answered no or are unsure, what is the main reason for your preference? Options include wanting to discuss treatment with your general practitioner before deciding, concerns about confidentiality, concerns about the cost of treatment, concerns about the adequacy of staff training, wanting more information before deciding, concerns about stigma and discrimination, or other (please specify). Please provide comments. 7. Task shifting refers to the process where certain tasks in hepatitis C testing and treatment are performed by a broader group of trained individuals rather than relying solely on specialists. The primary goal of task shifting is to make services more accessible to communities. 8. With whom would you prefer to discuss your health needs related to hepatitis C? Options include a specialist doctor, general practitioner, nurse, community-friendly medical personnel, community or peer worker, community leader, no preference, or other (please specify). 9. Who would you prefer to perform your hepatitis C test? Options include a specialist doctor, general practitioner, trained nurse, trained community or peer worker, community-friendly medical personnel, no preference, or other (please specify). Please provide reasons for your choice. 10. What is your primary reason for getting tested and, if applicable, eventually treated for hepatitis C? Options include better personal health, avoiding exposing family and friends to hepatitis C, being in good health to provide for and support your family, proximity of services, speed of services, trust in community or peer workers, trust in healthcare workers, trust in community leaders, national awareness campaigns, or other (please specify). 11. What is your primary reason for not getting tested and, if applicable, eventually treated for hepatitis C? Options include not feeling at risk, fear of learning your status, fear of stigma and discrimination from family and friends, fear of stigma and discrimination from healthcare personnel, direct costs (e.g., treatment and healthcare professional fees), indirect costs (e.g., loss of wages, transportation), distance of services, waiting times, or other (please specify). 12. Please rank the following factors in order of importance for making it easier for someone to be tested and treated for hepatitis C, from 1 (most important) to 7 (least important): having all necessary testing and treatment services in the same place; having all necessary testing and samples taken just once (e.g., if the first test is positive, a second confirmatory test is automatically done on the same sample); starting treatment on the same day as testing; having more local hepatitis C testing and treatment services (e.g., increasing availability outside big cities and hospitals); having hepatitis C testing and treatment services available where care is already provided for other health needs (e.g., primary care, HIV clinics, opioid substitution therapy centers, community-based organization centers); having hepatitis C testing and treatment services provided by trained non-specialist health workers; and having more information on hepatitis C, testing, and treatment. Please share your reasons for this ranking. 13. INPUD is a global, peer-based network that aims to promote the health and protect the rights and dignity of people who use or have used drugs, including those who inject drugs. 14. In April 2021, INPUD and other key population networks collaborated with the WHO Department of Global HIV, Hepatitis, and Sexually Transmitted Infection Programmes on a global qualitative study to inform the updating of the WHO 2016 consolidated guidelines for HIV prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care for key populations. For the first time, the updated guidelines will also address viral hepatitis and sexually transmitted infections. 15. The study involved four key populations: gay and bisexual men and other men who have sex with men, female, male, and transgender sex workers, people who inject drugs, and transgender people. The research explored their values and preferences regarding HIV, viral hepatitis, and STI interventions and programs. 16. Data were collected through individual semi-structured interviews and focus group discussions. Separate guides were developed for each method, and all research materials were piloted to ensure validity, accessibility, and suitability. 17. Participants were recruited using a purposive sampling approach to ensure diverse geography, gender, and age demographics. Eligibility criteria included being over 18 years old, providing oral informed consent, communicating in English, French, Spanish, or Russian (or via an interpreter), and identifying as a member of a key population or a key population organization/network. 18. All interviews and focus group discussions were conducted virtually using secure communication platforms. Data were collected by community experts engaged by global key population networks as consultants. Responses were documented, recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed using an inductive thematic analysis approach. 19. A total of 230 individuals from six WHO regions and 68 countries participated in the study. This included 61 semi-structured interviews and 32 focus group discussions. The findings were consolidated into a key population report and individual network reports for further analysis. 20. The study highlighted the importance of decentralization, integration, the role of peer workers, and addressing stigma and discrimination in hepatitis C service delivery. Community-led services were overwhelmingly preferred for their accessibility, confidentiality, and ability to provide safe spaces and relevant information. 21. Participants emphasized the need for integrating hepatitis C testing and treatment within broader harm-reduction approaches, including offering pangenotypic DAA treatment and prevention services in prisons. They also supported expanding treatment options and settings to maximize access and reduce barriers. 22. Effective community-led service models included drop-in centers, mobile clinics, peer outreach, and one-stop-shop models. Participants stressed the importance of training, support, and adequate resources to ensure high-quality service provision and best practices in clinical governance. 23. The study provided valuable insights into the values, preferences, and perceptions of key populations, offering data to inform the updating of the WHO guidelines and guide future research and service delivery approaches.
